questions.q: Why does an UPDATE statement need to both read and write the same row?
options: Reading happens only if the row doesn't already exist
UPDATE never reads anything; it only writes
UPDATE reads the whole table first, regardless of WHERE clause
It must first find the row to evaluate the WHERE clause, then change it — two separate operations back to back
questions.explain: Locating the row is a read; changing it is a write. That two-step nature is exactly what creates the deadlock risk update locks solve.

questions.q: What deadlock pattern would occur if UPDATE used a shared lock for its initial read-to-locate phase?
options: The two sessions would automatically merge their writes
Two sessions could both hold a shared lock on the same row and both wait forever to upgrade to exclusive
SQL Server would immediately roll back both sessions with no deadlock possible
Only the first session would ever be able to read the row
questions.explain: Shared locks are mutually compatible, so both sessions could hold one and then both be stuck waiting for the other's shared lock to clear before upgrading.

questions.q: What is an update (U) lock compatible with, and what is it NOT compatible with?
options: Compatible with everything, including another update lock
Not compatible with anything, including shared locks
Compatible with a shared (S) lock; not compatible with another update lock or an exclusive lock
Compatible only with an exclusive lock
questions.explain: U is compatible with S (so plain reads can proceed) but conflicts with another U and with X, so only one session at a time can be in the 'about to maybe update' phase.

questions.q: What happens to an update lock once SQL Server is ready to actually perform the write?
options: It converts to a schema modification lock
It converts to an exclusive (X) lock on that row
It is simply released with no further lock taken
It converts to a shared (S) lock
questions.explain: The update lock exists for the locate-the-row phase; once ready to write, it converts to an exclusive lock, held until COMMIT or ROLLBACK.

questions.q: Why do two concurrent UPDATE statements against the same row never deadlock against each other in normal use?
options: Because SQL Server always processes UPDATE statements in a fixed queue by session ID
Because UPDATE automatically retries instead of waiting
Because an update lock conflicts with another update lock, so only one session can be in that phase at a time — the second simply waits its turn
Because UPDATE statements always take a shared lock, which is compatible across sessions
questions.explain: The U-vs-U conflict is exactly the mechanism that closes the conversion-deadlock trap for ordinary concurrent UPDATE traffic.
